purpose: Compare rider price increases with agency service quality, state-of-good-repair delivery and audited spending using dated, comparable source series. A fare rise alone is not evidence of corruption.
rules: Do not label a proposed increase as adopted or an authorized capital plan as delivered infrastructure.
Separate operating revenue and spending from multi-year capital authorization, commitments, cash outlays and completed projects.
Compare service reliability only on the same metric, agency, service type and period; report year labels and methodology.
A 2025 service result cannot test the consequences of a fare change that begins in 2026.
An aggregate bus or rail indicator cannot establish the experience on a user's particular route, station, or commute.
A decline in service, high contractor cost or donor relationship does not alone demonstrate corruption or a price effect.
A large capital allocation is neither a cash expenditure nor a project completion. Commitments are legally binding obligations, not service improvements.
If verified fare trend, service outcome or capital execution evidence is missing, show a data gap rather than a fake performance score.

agencies.name: NYC subway and local bus
agencies.operator: Metropolitan Transportation Authority / New York City Transit
agencies.headline: Subway punctuality improved, but a large repair program still has a delivery gap.
agencies.ratingBasis: 2024–2025 weekday subway punctuality improved. The 2026 fare increase took effect after this outcome period; capital commitments remain materially below new five-year allocation.

fares.name: Subway/local bus full fare
fares.cadence: Fare rose in 2023 and again in January 2026; not annually in this example.

performance.name: Weekday subway terminal on-time performance
performance.method: MTA weekday terminal on-time performance; 2025 agency statement rounds to 1 decimal.
performance.interpretation: About 16.3% of 2025 weekday trains did not reach the terminal on time; performance varies by line and time of day. Both measurements precede the January 2026 fare increase.

capital.label: 2025–2029 capital plan
capital.scope: Entire MTA system, not just NYC subway
capital.warning: Plan allocation is not money spent. $7.5B committed as of April 2026 is not $7.5B of finished infrastructure. The program runs through 2029.

concerns.name: Maintenance contributes to existing delays
concerns.finding: NY State Comptroller reported that 31% of 2024 subway delays involved infrastructure/equipment and 25% involved planned maintenance.
concerns.warning: Not every infrastructure-related delay is caused by a failure to invest; planned work may cause short-term disruption.

nextMeasures: 2026 weekday on-time performance after fare increase
service interruptions and track speed restrictions by line
accessible stations and elevator availability
capital program cash spending and completed signal, fleet, station projects
contract-level payment and audit records
agencies.action: Compare your actual line’s on-time trend with the MTA board's fare decision and the independently tracked project schedule.

sources.label: NY State Comptroller debt and capital analysis

agencies.name: NJ Transit rail and bus
agencies.headline: Fares rose while both reported systemwide rail and bus punctuality were lower than FY2023.
agencies.ratingBasis: FY2023 versus FY2025 published systemwide on-time performance fell. Fare increases began July 2024. Neither comparison alone identifies the cause.

fares.name: Systemwide fare adjustment
fares.cadence: 15% adjustment; indexed to a base of 100, not an actual ticket amount. Separate 3% annual adjustments scheduled starting July 2025.
fares.warning: Initial public-hearing notice is a proposal source; the 2026 board budget separately confirms the 3% fare increase scheduled for July 2026.

fares.name: Scheduled annual percentage adjustment
fares.cadence: Proposed/assumed by 2026 budget: 3% in July 2026, with similar annual adjustments anticipated; route prices and rounding vary.

performance.name: Systemwide rail on-time performance
performance.method: NJ Transit systemwide rail OTP (all delay causes), reported in its FY2023 progress summary and FY2025 annual report.
performance.interpretation: A 2.9-percentage-point deterioration, despite fare adjustments in the intervening period. Amtrak-owned infrastructure, weather, fleet and scheduling may also influence the outcome.

performance.name: Systemwide bus on-time performance
performance.method: NJ Transit published FY2023 and FY2025 bus on-time performance.
performance.interpretation: A decline of 3 percentage points; weather, traffic, staffing and fleet reliability may affect results. Station-specific performance requires a separate route-level series.

concerns.name: FY2027 operating-budget pressure
concerns.finding: NJ Transit’s April 2026 board documents projected an 11% increase in expenditures, citing labor, services, materials and supplies; the 3% fare increase was expected to offset farebox revenue below forecast.
concerns.warning: This is the agency budget rationale, not an independent verification of efficiency or the performance consequences of the increase.

nextMeasures: Verified by-route OTP and cancellations before/after each increase
actual capital spending and station/track asset condition by project
fare revenue growth versus operating costs and riders carried
avoidable delays by NJ Transit versus Amtrak infrastructure
project bid prices, amendments and inspector-general findings
agencies.action: Use NJ Transit's downloadable route-level performance tables and match them to a specific fare change, not a systemwide claim about every trip.

sources.label: NJT route and system performance downloads

agencies.name: PATH rail
agencies.operator: Port Authority of New York and New Jersey
agencies.headline: Scheduled fare increases accompany promised service and infrastructure investment; delivery needs verification.
agencies.ratingBasis: Public 2026–2035 capital plan and PATH fare schedule are available, but no comparable, fully validated before-and-after route reliability series was obtained.

fares.name: PATH single ride
fares.cadence: $0.25 fare increase in 2026, with further planned $0.25 steps through 2029.

capital.label: Planned PATH investment, 2026–2035
capital.scope: PATH-only planned allocations in the Port Authority capital plan
capital.warning: A 10-year allocation is not a completion record. Number of added trains, weekend frequency, and updated accessible stations must be checked as projects are delivered.

concerns.name: Subsidy context
concerns.finding: The Port Authority says PATH fares cover approximately 25% of operating cost per ride, with the balance subsidized. The announced fare increases accompany plans for more frequent weekday and weekend service.
concerns.warning: The farebox cost-recovery percentage comes from the agency and is not evidence of outcomes.

nextMeasures: PATH actual trains/hour by day and station
end-to-end travel-time reliability and unplanned outages
delivered versus promised weekend service increases
capital commitments, cash outlays and completed station renewal work
operating subsidies and farebox recovery over time
agencies.action: Compare the published PATH timetable and actual service against the 2026–2035 capital plan, then check whether each fare increase delivered the promised additional train service.

agencies.name: Port Authority bridges and tunnels
agencies.operator: Port Authority of New York and New Jersey
agencies.headline: Automatic toll adjustments are documented; promised infrastructure value needs crossing-level delivery evidence.
agencies.ratingBasis: 2026 budget explains revenue and annual CPI adjustments, and capital plan lists bridge/tunnel work; actual crossing-by-crossing improvements require dated completed-project and travel-time indicators.

fares.name: Peak auto E-ZPass CPI adjustment
fares.cadence: Additional $0.48 peak-auto CPI adjustment from 2025 rate, alongside previously authorized fixed toll adjustments. This is the increment, not the full toll price.

capital.label: Port Authority TB&T plan allocation, 2026–2035
capital.scope: Bridges, tunnels and bus terminal, including approximately $11B for a Midtown Bus Terminal; not a crossing-only maintenance budget
capital.warning: The $15.4B category includes a major bus terminal and multiple projects; it cannot be treated as spending on a particular bridge or tunnel.

concerns.name: 2026 toll revenue forecast
concerns.finding: The 2026 Port Authority budget projects about $2.3B in bridge-and-tunnel toll revenue, $123M or 5.8% above the 2025 budget, from several factors including CPI adjustments.
concerns.warning: Projected revenues are not proof of realized cash collection or a completed road improvement.

nextMeasures: Crossing-specific travel time, incident rates and closures
bridge and tunnel inspection deficiencies resolved
capital contract awards, completion certificates and approved change orders
toll revenue allocated to specific facilities versus cross-subsidies
cost per project and auditor recommendations
agencies.action: Compare each toll-setting vote with the specific crossing’s published capital commitments, completed repairs and travel-time trends.

sources.label: Port Authority tolls and published policy

agencies.name: Chicago CTA buses and trains
agencies.headline: CTA fares did not increase every year; the agency retained its base fare through 2026.
agencies.ratingBasis: Agency's 2026 fare schedule retained base fares; independent yearly performance-to-spending matching needs more detailed time series.

fares.name: CTA standard 'L' rail fare
fares.cadence: Unchanged base rail fare from 2018 through 2026; a 2025 proposed 2026 fare hike was not adopted.

capital.label: 2026 capital budget
capital.scope: CTA agencywide 2026 capital budget, not completed infrastructure
capital.warning: Budget dollars do not show infrastructure completions or actual cash expenditures.

concerns.name: Budget and public performance context
concerns.finding: CTA reports a $2.231B operating budget and $1.505B capital budget for 2026 and publishes monthly performance dashboard reports.
concerns.warning: This annual budget does not establish changes in punctuality, safety, station condition or track restrictions.

nextMeasures: Monthly service delivery, headways and passenger wait time by rail line and bus route
rail slow-zone miles and equipment failure rates
bus reliability and staffing by garage
capital contracts completed versus dollars planned
crowding and accessibility changes by station
agencies.action: Use CTA's monthly performance dashboard and the planned-versus-completed capital budget to test whether a given line improved.

national.title: No single national fare or infrastructure-return score
national.finding: The FTA National Transit Database and transit asset condition program can identify useful service and state-of-good-repair metrics. Fares, capital projects, operating budgets and asset condition must be matched to a named operator and time period.
framework: Percent of vehicles exceeding useful life benchmark
Percent of facilities in poor condition
Fare per paid boarding and full trip cost
Capital commitments, actual spending and completed projects

followTheMoney.question: Did higher prices deliver better, safer, more reliable transportation?

checks.title: Price
checks.question: Which exact fare or toll changed and when?
checks.evidence: Official before-and-after rate schedules, rider eligibility and transfer rules

checks.title: Service
checks.question: Did the same route become more reliable and accessible?
checks.evidence: Matched route-specific OTP, cancellations, speed restrictions, outages and accessible stations

checks.title: Delivery
checks.question: Were infrastructure promises actually completed?
checks.evidence: Approved capital plan, contracted commitments, invoices, completion dates, physical asset-condition change

checks.title: Accountability
checks.question: Could avoidable waste or a conflict have affected the rate?
checks.evidence: Original contract IDs, bid evaluations, change orders, inspector-general report, financing, board fare vote

followTheMoney.warning: Do not use a planned billion-dollar capital program as a proxy for infrastructure improvement; do not use a fare hike as proof of corruption.
